description: Fictional English design review with a reversed download decision, reassigned implementation, corrected deadlines and unresolved file retention.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Let's settle how the new export button should behave. Our provisional plan is to create the file immediately and keep the user on the results page.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That would be the simplest screen. I can show a spinner beside the button, then replace it with a download link when the file is ready.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: I need to challenge that assumption. A large request can take almost a minute, and the browser connection may close before the server finishes.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Would a higher timeout solve that, or would we just make people wait longer without knowing whether their request had actually been accepted?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: We'd mostly hide the problem. If someone presses the button twice, they might start two jobs, and the screen wouldn't explain which one completed.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Then let's replace the immediate download with a queued job. The page should confirm acceptance straight away and show a separate status for completion.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Agreed. I'll build the server endpoint and the progress screen. I originally estimated Friday afternoon, but I think we can finish both on Thursday.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: You still don't have permission to deploy that service. I can take the endpoint, including duplicate request protection, while you handle the progress screen.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That division makes sense. The endpoint moves to you. Please give us a specific delivery time so the screen can be tested against it.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: I'll put it in the test environment on Wednesday at three in the afternoon. The first response will contain a job identifier and a status URL.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Then I'll deliver the screen on Thursday at eleven. Sorry, make that ten in the morning; the review starts at eleven, so it needs to be ready earlier.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Thursday at ten is the committed time. The eleven o'clock slot is for review. We'll remove Friday afternoon from the plan so nobody follows the old estimate.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Should we send an email when the job finishes? People may close the page, especially if they started the export just before leaving their desk.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Let's defer email notifications. For this release, the results page will list recent jobs, and users can return there to collect a finished file.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: What should the screen say if a job fails? I don't want a generic success message just because the request was accepted by the queue.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Accepted and completed must stay separate. A failed job gets an error status, and retrying it should create a fresh request after the user confirms.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Good. Please include that distinction in the test checklist. A successful request is not evidence that a usable export file has been produced.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: One remaining question is how long those files stay available. I was going to display seven days, but we haven't checked the storage policy.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Leave that duration out of the interface for now. The retention period is still unresolved, and we shouldn't turn an estimate into a promise.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Understood. My screen is due Thursday at ten, email is deferred, and the retention message stays undecided until the policy review is complete.
